sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] Ten turns, all within the word limits. [s2] Nine turns, each within 25-65 words. [s3] All turns fall within 25-65 words and the length is even.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention

sub.limitation: [s1] The turn 9 reversal is undercut by the misattribution.

sub.limitation: [s1] The Meaning Seeker sounds generic and is barely Frankl. [s2] The Reductionist and the Analyst are generic. [s3] The prose is uniformly polite and textbook-like.

sub.name: Memorable delivery

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement

sub.example: [s2] Turn 8 unexpectedly warns against over-mastering sleep. [s3] Turn 6 turns to meaning and boredom as a source of fatigue.
sub.limitation: [s2] Turn 7's reversal makes no sense, so it doesn't land. [s3] Turn 7's concession is mild and expected.

strengths: [s1] Turn 10 names a decisive, checkable condition (snoring or gasping) as the missing fact.
[s1] Turn 7 sets a concrete 14-day experiment with an explicit point to escalate to a doctor.
[s1] Turn 8's objection that tracking could raise stress is new and holds up.
[s2] Medically more specific: sleep architecture (turn 1) and apnea versus temperature (turn 4).
[s2] Section E gives concrete warning signs and a two-week log to tell the paths apart.
[s2] Minds mostly address each other by name, which helps the reader follow.
[s3] Turn 10 asks a sharp, answerable question that separates body from meaning.
[s3] Section E gives concrete apnea red flags: snoring, gasping, morning headaches.
[s3] Turn 7 makes an explicit concession that narrows the claim rather than moving the goalposts.
weaknesses: [s1] Turn 9 credits the Meaning Seeker with the Architect's turn 4 point, a revision that misattributes.
[s1] The Meaning Seeker (turns 3, 5) attributes 'lethargy as protective barrier' to Frankl without support.
[s1] Medically narrow: only apnea is considered, with no mention of thyroid, anemia, mood or medication.
[s2] Turn 7: the Reductionist retracts 'environment is the culprit', a claim he never made.
[s2] Turn 2 presents a modern paraphrase of Meditations 5.16 as a quotation; the year 161 is wrong.
[s2] Turn 9 (the Stoic) turns a medical question into valuing 'internal clarity'.
[s3] Turn 9 overstates the danger of a 7-day log; tracking and a doctor's visit could run together.
[s3] Existential Skeptic turns 3 and 6 are asserted, unanswered, and close to speculating about motives.
[s3] No other medical causes (iron, thyroid, mood) and no question about how long it has lasted.
editorNotes: [s1] Require every concession to quote or name the exact turn and speaker that prompted it.
[s1] For health questions, require the medical mind to name a short list of common treatable causes and red flags.
[s1] Forbid a mind from attributing a mechanism to its author unless the book actually argues it.
[s2] Require concessions to quote the speaker's own earlier turn number, so revisions stay coherent.
[s2] Require quotations to match a named public-domain translation exactly, or be paraphrased without quotation marks.
[s2] Make the closing turn answer the user's actual question, such as when to get checked, not a values abstraction.
[s2] Tell the clinical mind to name the full routine-checkup list, not only apnea.
[s3] Require one turn that asks how long the problem has lasted and checks other red flags.
[s3] Require that every mind answers the strongest objection made against it.
[s3] Ask for the next steps to combine options when they do not conflict, such as logging plus a GP visit.
[s3] Enforce consistent pd flags for every turn that cites a pre-1931 book.

sub.name: Faithful engagement

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] Section D frames the choice as observe first versus test now. [s2] Options: see a doctor, change routines, re-evaluate goals, or log for a week. [s3] Track, fix the environment, accept, or see a doctor all appear.
sub.limitation: [s1] Does not offer limited steps such as seeing a GP for bloodwork. [s2] Frames doctor and re-evaluation as competing when both can be done. [s3] The acceptance option in turn 3 is not developed as a real choice.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 names the cost of delay; turn 5 the cost of rushing to blame the body. [s2] Turn 6 warns that optimizing may hide burnout. [s3] Turn 7 notes that focusing on tracking may miss medical urgency.
sub.limitation: [s1] The costs of testing (time, money, anxiety) are not discussed. [s2] No cost, time or risk given for getting checked versus waiting. [s3] No option's cost in time, money or suffering is spelled out.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E: snoring or gasping makes testing urgent. [s2] Section E: snoring or gasping makes a medical check the priority. [s3] Section E: snoring or gasping make medical evaluation the priority.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 9's broken-component-versus-system test gives the user nothing to check. [s2] Leaves out other red flags such as daytime sleepiness while driving or low mood. [s3] The debate turns give no decisive conditions, only section E.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 admits the question 'remains an open question'. [s2] Turn 10 names the cause as the open question. [s3] Section D names two causes that need different approaches.
sub.limitation: [s1] It then overclaims that a sleep study alone resolves it. [s2] Does not rank which unknowns matter most. [s3] Major unknowns are not separated from minor ones.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: [s1] Section E: a one-week sleep journal taken to a healthcare provider. [s2] Section E: log both physical rest and sense of purpose for a week. [s3] A 30-day sleep hygiene trial with dark, cool room and no screens.
sub.limitation: [s1] The one-week journal conflicts with the 14 days in turns 5-6, with no explanation. [s2] Never says the plain step: a routine GP visit is cheap. [s3] A month's wait without red flags is long and conflicts with turn 7's urgency.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] 'Sleep duration is only half the battle' is plain and clear. [s2] Plain wording throughout, e.g. turn 8's 'mechanical failure'. [s3] Short, plain sentences throughout.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 2's 'nature-aligned rest' is vague. [s2] Turn 3's 'internal batteries' and 'aimlessness' stay vague. [s3] 'Sleep latency' in turn 1 is unexplained.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] Most turns name the speaker they are answering. [s2] Turn 7 names the Existential Skeptic as the source of the concession. [s3] Turns 4-6 attribute the claims they answer.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 7's causal link back to turn 6 is hard to follow. [s2] 'You' moves between the user and other minds; turn 10's 'You disagree' is unclear. [s3] Turn 6's 'if that is the case' does not follow from mismatch.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] Nine short turns, all within limits. [s2] Ten turns, each within 25-65 words. [s3] Turns are brief and all within 25-65 words.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8 slows the pace without adding much. [s2] The turns are evenly matched in length, which flattens the rhythm. [s3] Turns run near the 25-word minimum and feel thin.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] The Systems Thinker brings a distinct lens of loops and environment. [s2] Three clearly separate lenses: biology, systems, meaning. [s3] The Stoic stands apart in turns 3 and 6.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Stoic's position drifts between turns 2, 5 and 8 without being marked. [s2] The voices sound alike; every turn opens with a 'You ... but' structure. [s3] Turn 7's switch blurs the Data Optimizer's position.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] Section E has three clear arrow-led branches. [s2] Section E summarizes the debate in three useful sentences. [s3] There is little repetition across the nine turns.
sub.limitation: [s1] Apnea is repeated in turns 4 and 7 and in both D and E. [s2] The Skeptic's turns 3, 6 and 9 repeat the same claim. [s3] Section D partly repeats Section A.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6's warning about worsening burnout raises the stakes. [s2] Turn 8: a 'mechanical failure that no amount of purpose can overcome'. [s3] Turn 7 raises 'the urgency of a potential medical issue'.
sub.limitation: [s1] The stakes rest on an assumed high-pressure job. [s2] The tension is stated rather than built. [s3] Stakes are named rather than felt.

sub.name: Surprise and plausible reversals
sub.example: [s1] In turn 7 the Realist pivots to urgent screening.
sub.limitation: [s1] The reversal feels unmotivated rather than earned.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] The Stoic's sternness in turn 8 is in character. [s2] The Skeptic's 'optimizing the path toward deeper burnout' (turn 6). [s3] The Stoic in turn 3 says the body is 'a vessel subject to decay'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Voices are generic; there is little of Marcus or Meadows in the phrasing. [s2] No mind sounds like its author; all three are generic. [s3] The Data Optimizer and the Biologist sound generic.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] Turn 3's stress-to-poor-sleep-to-stress loop is the one vivid image. [s2] Turn 9: 'treat your body purely like a machine to be repaired'. [s3] Turn 5: 'a logbook will not save you.'
sub.limitation: [s1] No analogies, examples or sharp lines. [s2] No vivid example, analogy or concrete scene. [s3] The memorable lines are dismissive rather than illuminating.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] Moves from habits to urgency to an open question. [s2] Turns 8-10 lead to a stated open question. [s3] The arc moves toward the apnea concern in turn 8.
sub.limitation: [s1] The flat tone gives little emotional arc. [s2] Flat rhythm: every turn has the same intensity. [s3] It ends on 'lack of discipline', which is flat and slightly scolding.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s2] Turn 7: the Architect gives up the claim that habits are enough. [s3] Turn 7's sudden reversal.
sub.limitation: [s2] This is the only shift in the whole debate. [s3] The reversal is implausible because nothing caused it.

strengths: [s1] Turns 5-7 debate a real sequencing question: observe for 14 days or get screened now.
[s1] Turn 6 names a concrete cost of delay, a rare instance of weighing tradeoffs.
[s1] Section E's branches are short, clear conditions the user could act on.
[s2] Turn 7 is a real, credited concession that merges tracking of environment and stress.
[s2] Section E gives clear decisive conditions: snoring or gasping means getting checked first.
[s2] Turn 1 usefully moves the focus from sleep quantity to sleep quality.
[s3] Section E gives clear snoring and gasping red flags for medical priority.
[s3] Turn 6 reframes seeing a doctor as rational agency rather than giving up.
[s3] Turns are concise and easy to follow.
weaknesses: [s1] Turn 7's revision is a non sequitur: outside pressures are no reason for immediate medical screening.
[s1] Turn 2 (Stoic) suggests brief rest can suffice, which is misleading health advice.
[s1] Turn 9 overclaims that only a sleep study could settle a question about stress.
[s2] The Existential Skeptic repeats the meaning-deficit point (turns 3, 6, 9) on invented context.
[s2] The Reductionist leans on James's 1890 Principles for apnea and circadian claims, a poor fit as grounding.
[s2] Turn 5 strawmans turn 4 ('biology is the only hurdle'), and turn 10's 'You disagree' is ambiguous.
[s3] Data Optimizer turn 7 reverses with no prompting, so it reads as forced agreement.
[s3] Stoic turns 3 and 9 suggest accepting tiredness or a lack of discipline, which is unhelpful and moralising.
[s3] The Evolutionary Biologist's Part 4 and 5 bases look unreliable, and turn 8 introduces apnea without a link to earlier turns.
editorNotes: [s1] Require each change of position to give a reason that actually follows from the cited turn.
[s1] Ban invented user details (for example a high-pressure job); turn them into conditional questions instead.
[s1] Require section E's next steps to match the timeframes the debate proposed.
[s1] For health questions, forbid minds from minimising rest needs or treating possible illness as a test of attitude.
[s2] Require each mind's source to actually cover its claims; prefer a modern clinical source for medical claims.
[s2] Ban speculation about the user's life such as 'empty work' unless framed as a question to the user.
[s2] Require each mind to revise or concede at least once, and forbid repeating a point without new content.
[s2] Require the speaker to name who 'you' refers to when addressing another mind.
[s3] Require that a concession cite the specific earlier argument that caused it.
[s3] Ban framings that moralise symptoms, such as discipline or acceptance, when a medical cause is plausible.
[s3] Require at least one question to the user inside the debate turns.
[s3] Require basis references to real chapters or parts of the cited book.
